text: You are asleep. It is half past eleven at night.
Under your bed there is carpet, and under the carpet a slab of concrete.
Under the concrete there is sand.
Rain picks up carbon dioxide on the way down, which makes it very slightly acidic.
Limestone dissolves in slightly acidic water. Not quickly. But it never stops.
So under the sand there is limestone, and it has been quietly going away for forty thousand years.
Tonight it finishes.
The hole that opened under Jeffrey Bush in Seffner, Florida, was about six metres across.
His brother heard him shout, ran in, and started digging with his hands.
A sheriff's deputy pulled the brother back out as the floor kept going.
Jeffrey was never recovered. The house was demolished and the hole was filled with gravel.
There was no crack. No creak. No warning of any kind.
Limestone does not announce itself. It just stops holding.
That is the ground. Let's keep you alive and go outside.
You are standing on the shore of a lake in Cameroon. It is a beautiful lake.
It is also two hundred metres deep, and it sits in the throat of a dead volcano.
Carbon dioxide seeps up from the magma below and dissolves into the cold water at the bottom.
The weight of the water above holds it there. For years. For decades.
Then something disturbs it. A landslip. A cold night. Nobody is sure which.
The deep water rises a few metres — and the gas comes out of it like a shaken bottle.
A column of carbon dioxide a hundred metres high leaves the lake in about twenty seconds.
It is heavier than air. So it does not rise and disperse. It pours downhill.
It goes into the valleys at about seventy kilometres an hour, and it fills them.
You do not smell it. You do not choke. There is simply no oxygen in the breath you just took.
At Lake Nyos in nineteen eighty-six that killed one thousand seven hundred and forty-six people, and every animal for twenty-five kilometres.
Almost nobody woke up.
Three lakes on Earth are known to do this. Nyos, Monoun, and Kivu.
Kivu holds about a thousand times more gas, and two million people live around it.
Nyos now has pipes in it, venting the gas on purpose, forever.
Turn around. There is a hill behind the town.
It has been smoking for two weeks and everybody has got used to it.
In Saint-Pierre, Martinique, in nineteen oh two, there was an election coming, and the newspaper said the mountain was nothing to worry about.
On the eighth of May the side of the mountain gives way.
What comes out is not lava. Lava you can walk away from.
This is rock, ash and gas at around a thousand degrees, moving as one fluid.
It behaves like a liquid because it is denser than the air it is shoving out of the way.
It reaches the town in about a minute, at roughly six hundred kilometres an hour.
It does not burn you the way fire burns you. It is far too fast for that.
At Herculaneum, researchers found skulls where the brain tissue had turned to glass.
That takes a temperature spike of several hundred degrees and then an almost instant cooling.
Saint-Pierre had about twenty-eight thousand people in it. The flow took under a minute.
Two survived. One of them, Ludger Sylbaris, was in an underground cell with one small grated window.
He had been locked up the night before, after a fight.
He was badly burned through the grate, and he lived. He later toured with a circus.
Now stand by a lake with no volcano anywhere near it. Scotland will do.
It is a still day. Nothing is happening here at all.
Two thousand kilometres south, the seabed off Portugal moves, and Lisbon is destroyed.
The shaking that reaches Scotland is far too gentle for anyone to feel.
But it arrives at almost exactly the rate the loch likes to rock at.
Every body of water has a rhythm it wants to rock at. A bath has one. A loch has one.
Like a hand pushing a swing at the right moment, over and over.
The whole loch tilts. The water climbs one end and falls away from the other.
In seventeen fifty-five, people across Scotland watched calm lochs stand up and start swinging.
After the Japanese earthquake of twenty eleven, Norwegian fjords did the same thing about thirty minutes later.
It is called a seiche. It needs no wave, no tsunami, and no earthquake anywhere near you.
Boats were torn off their moorings in water that had felt nothing.
Go deeper. Not under the house — under the continent.
A supervolcano is not a mountain. It is a chamber of part-molten rock the size of a county.
Toba, in Sumatra, erupted about seventy-four thousand years ago and left a caldera you can see from orbit.
And here is where you have probably been told something that is not true.
The story goes that Toba nearly wiped out humanity, and that everyone alive descends from a few thousand survivors.
Whole-genome sequencing does not find that crash. And archaeological sites either side of the ash layer show people simply carrying on.
The eruption was real and enormous. The near-extinction is not supported.
There is something else about supervolcanoes nobody mentions.
Of everything on this list, it is the one that would give you the most warning.
Filling a chamber that size lifts the ground and sets off months of earthquake swarms. You would see it coming for a very long time.
The one everybody is frightened of is the one you could walk away from.
Keep going out. Ninety-three million miles out.
The sun throws a billion tonnes of charged particles into space. Sometimes at us.
On the first of September eighteen fifty-nine, Richard Carrington watched a white flare cross a sunspot.
Seventeen hours later the aurora reached the Caribbean. People in Boston read newspapers by it at one in the morning.
Telegraph lines threw sparks. Some operators were shocked. Some paper caught fire.
And a few operators found they could disconnect their batteries entirely and keep sending — the aurora was powering the line.
In eighteen fifty-nine there were about a hundred and twenty thousand miles of telegraph wire in the world.
Now picture the same storm hitting a planet wired end to end.
The transformers at risk are the very large ones, and they are built to order.
Water treatment stops. Fuel pumps stop. Payment systems stop. Refrigeration stops.
A replacement can take a year or more to arrive. There is no warehouse full of spares.
And every country that needs one is ordering at the same moment.
The warning, if we spot the flare, is about seventeen hours. Which sounds generous.
Seventeen hours is enough to take a grid offline on purpose. It is not enough to rewire a country.
One more step out. All the way out.
A star far bigger than ours runs out of fuel and collapses.
It fires two narrow beams from its poles, and in a few seconds each beam carries more energy than our sun will make in its entire life.
The beams are narrow. That is the only reason this is rare rather than routine.
Point one at Earth from close enough, and nothing in the way makes any difference at all.
In October twenty twenty-two one of them arrived, from one point nine billion light years away.
It was bright enough to disturb the upper atmosphere of this planet. From one point nine billion light years.
If one happened close, and pointed the right way, it would strip ozone off an entire hemisphere.
The warning would be the light itself.
It travels at the speed of light. So does the information that it is coming.
There is no warning. There is no version of this where there is warning.
The ground under your feet. The lake. The hill. The water. The rock. The star. And the thing outside it all.
Most of it will never happen to you.
But it is all happening somewhere, to somebody, roughly on schedule.
Sleep well.
